power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: To address these issues, we recruited the largest cohort of systematically evaluated individuals with 3q29del and 3q29dup to date: we evaluated 103 3q29del carriers and 38 3q29dup carriers.

Individuals with 3q29del (n=103, 58.25% male, 16.98±11.17 years old) or 3q29dup (n=38, 55.26% male, 20.34±13.67 years old) were recruited from the existing online 3q29 registry (3q29deletion.com) (5), as well as direct referrals and contacts.

Typically developing controls (n=54, 42.59% male, 17.85±10.66 years old) and their relatives (n=45, 11.11% male, 46.09±8.16 years old) were recruited from community sources and from ResearchMatch, an online platform for individuals interested in participating in research (54).

Participants are rated on a scale of 0-6 across positive, negative, disorganized, and general symptom domains, with scores of 3-5 on any positive symptom domain item indicating CHR, and a score of 6 on any positive symptom domain item indicating psychosis.

C1 means that the participant completed the task with good effort and understanding throughout, C2 means the participant completed the task with good effort on at least 50% of the task items, and C3 means the participant completed the task with good effort on less than 50% of the task items.
The accuracy score for each task corresponds to the number of items the participant completed correctly for the task.
We found that 3q29del participants had significant deficits compared to controls across all Penn-CNB domains for efficiency and accuracy (Figure 3A-B, Table S2, Table S3).

Penn-CNB domain-and task-specific deficits in 3q29dup 3q29dup participants had significant deficits compared to controls across all Penn-CNB domains for both efficiency and accuracy (Figure 3A-B, Table S2, Table S3).

However, this does not appear to hold true in 3q29del; even though individuals with 3q29del are at increased risk for ADHD (17), our subjects with 3q29del exhibit both decreased accuracy and decreased response speed relative to controls and subjects with 3q29dup.
